Supervisor of Elections, Ana Mataiciwa, appeared on fijivillage Straight Talk With Vijay Narayan.

The show focused on the state of preparedness of the Fijian Elections Office for the proposed national referendum on December 9th and the next general elections which has to be held by February 6th 2027, the nationwide voter registration underway, changes to the electoral laws and the impact on the voters and the country, and the impact of any drastic changes with two months to go for the last day for the Writ of Elections to be issued on December 24th 2026 amongst other issues.

item.title: Levuidali files Online Safety Commission complaint against Bainivalu over alleged cyber-bullying
item.description: Ba business owner Sevanaia Levuidali has filed a complaint with the Online Safety Commission (OSC) against Minister for Fisheries and Forestry Alitia Bainivalu, accusing her of cyber-bullying after she posted a video of him falling off a chair during a public consultation. When asked by fijivillage News whether the Commission has received Levuidali’s complaint, Commissioner Filipe Batiwale says th
item.content:encoded:
Ba business owner Sevanaia Levuidali has filed a complaint with the Online Safety Commission (OSC) against Minister for Fisheries and Forestry Alitia Bainivalu, accusing her of cyber-bullying after she posted a video of him falling off a chair during a public consultation.

When asked by fijivillage News whether the Commission has received Levuidali’s complaint, Commissioner Filipe Batiwale says the Commission respects the privacy and confidentiality of individuals who approach the organisation and does not ordinarily confirm or discuss individual complaints without an appropriate basis.

Batiwale says the Commission treats matters brought to its attention impartially and in accordance with the Online Safety Act 2018, irrespective of the individuals involved.

Meanwhile, Batiwale has also requested that the circumstances surrounding a laughing reaction attributed to the Commission’s official facebook account be established, after it appeared under a comment about Levuidali falling off a chair.

The laughing reaction appeared under a comment on a video shared by Bainivalu, showing Levuidali falling off a chair while making a submission to the Joint Committee on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2026 in Ba.

Levuidali has also filed a report at the Ba Police Station against Bainivalu over the incident, with Police confirming the report to fijivillage News.

The complaint follows Bainivalu’s posting of a video on her official facebook page showing Levuidali falling off his chair while making a submission to the Joint Committee on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2026 at the Ba Market Bure.

The video is taken from a Fiji Government livestream of the public consultation.

Speaking to fijivillage News, Levuidali questions why Bainivalu chooses to share the footage showing him falling off the chair.

He raises concerns about cyber-bullying and the use of social media by public figures, also referring to previous incidents involving members of Government.

In response, Bainivalu says she does not intend to ridicule Levuidali and has been posting videos of the public consultations over the past week.

She says Levuidali is not singled out, adding that the video also shows the part of his submission in which he ridicules the panel.

Bainivalu says the consultations are public hearings that allow people to engage in different forms of discussion .

She adds that it is unfortunate Levuidali falls off his chair and says the videos are intended to show the public that the consultations are open to everyone, regardless of whether they sit, stand or speak while facing away from the panel .

Bainivalu also says people should prepare themselves well before attending the consultations.

item.title: 50 men, five women: PM Rogers questions gender imbalance during Fiji Women’s Practice Parliament
item.description: Women must have equal opportunities to lead in Parliament, corporate boardrooms and senior management, with transparent selection processes, practical support and accountability needed to address their under-representation. This has been highlighted by Annie Rogers, who took on the role of Prime Minister and Minister for Civil Service and Strategic Planning, National Development and Statistics, an
item.content:encoded:
Women must have equal opportunities to lead in Parliament, corporate boardrooms and senior management, with transparent selection processes, practical support and accountability needed to address their under-representation.

This has been highlighted by Annie Rogers, who took on the role of Prime Minister and Minister for Civil Service and Strategic Planning, National Development and Statistics, and Public Enterprise during the Fiji Women's Practice Parliament session this morning.

Rogers pointed to the current composition of Fiji's Parliament, which has 50 men and five women, questioning whether leadership opportunities were being distributed fairly between men and women.

She says the figures raised serious questions about the recognition of women's ability, intelligence and leadership potential.

Rogers says Fiji can not afford to waste talent by holding capable women back from leadership positions.

She stresses that women are citizens who deserve representation, not merely voters whose support was sought during elections.

Rogers say women's experiences can strengthen decision-making across all areas, including the economy, infrastructure, national security, climate resilience, public finance and health.

She also called for greater transparency in appointments to corporate boards and chief executive positions, saying qualified women should not be overlooked because leadership continued to be viewed as a male role.

Rogers describes women's representation in leadership as an economic, governance and democratic issue.

She proposed four commitments to improve women's access to leadership.

These include establishing transparent pathways into leadership, providing practical support such as mentoring and leadership development, introducing published targets and regular reporting on women's representation, and giving serious consideration to temporary special measures through consultation and a lawful process.

Rogers says political parties, companies and public institutions must actively seek qualified women and examine how candidates were selected, supported and promoted.

She also highlighted the need for campaign resources and arrangements that recognise caring responsibilities, stressing that men must share those responsibilities.

On accountability, Rogers proposed regular reporting on women's representation in public appointments, boards and senior management, while encouraging businesses and political parties to adopt similar measures.

Addressing concerns about merit, she says men did not have a monopoly on merit and should therefore not have a monopoly on opportunity.

Rogers says the way women are treated in leadership positions also shaped how the next generation viewed equality.

She is urging Parliament to ensure girls could see leadership as a responsibility they could aspire to and realistically attain, while boys learned that women should be treated as equals.

item.title: 15-year-old raises concerns that moderate chastisement provision could expose children to further abuse
item.description: 15-year-old Hosanna Waqairapoa is concerned that the provision on moderate chastisement in the Constitution Amendment Bill could allow teachers, fellow students and family members to punish children. Speaking during the consultations in Nakasi, Waqairapoa says the proposed clause states that she could be subjected to moderate and lawful chastisement.
item.content:encoded:
15-year-old Hosanna Waqairapoa is concerned that the provision on moderate chastisement in the Constitution Amendment Bill could allow teachers, fellow students and family members to punish children.

Speaking during the consultations in Nakasi, Waqairapoa says the proposed clause states that she could be subjected to moderate and lawful chastisement.

She questioned what the words "moderate" and "lawful" mean.

Waqairapoa says the provision could be used to justify the abuse of children by parents, teachers, fellow students and others who exploit them.

She says there have been numerous reports of children being subjected to physical and sexual abuse.

Waqairapoa who is a Saint Joseph's Secondary School student further says that many cases of child abuse have been reported in the past year alone, and she fears that including a provision for moderate and lawful chastisement in the Constitution could create further opportunities for children to be abused.

The 15-year-old highlighted the importance of Christian principles, saying they should encourage people to respect, care for and love one another, particularly children.

However, she stressed that Christianity should not be forced upon anyone, as religious belief must be a matter of personal choice.

She says forcing someone to become a Christian through the law would be meaningless and contrary to Christian teachings.

item.title: Police currently taking statements after suspected drugs found on Yadua Island
item.description: Police are currently taking statements following the discovery of a parcel containing a white powdered substance believed to be illicit drugs on Yadua Island in Bua yesterday. Police say the parcel was found by a villager along the seashore.
item.content:encoded:
Police are currently taking statements following the discovery of a parcel containing a white powdered substance believed to be illicit drugs on Yadua Island in Bua yesterday.

Police say the parcel was found by a villager along the seashore.

The parcel was handed over to the village headman, who took it to Nabouwalu Police Station and reported the matter.

Police say the parcel is in their custody as they await further analysis.

Members of the public are urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 919 or the Police Call Centre on 1681 if they come across similar findings.
